newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN to deploy Guatemala peacekeepers by February.
newsitem.headline: UN to deploy Guatemala peacekeepers by February.

text.p: The United Nations on Tuesday made plans to send 155 peacekeepers to Guatemala, after China lifted its veto on military observers to monitor peace accords in the Central American country.
U.N. spokesman Fred Eckhard said there appeared to be no problem in getting the required number of observers "which can be deployed by early to mid-February."

On Monday the Security Council, including China, voted unanimously to dispatch the peacekeepers following days of confusion after China on January 10 used its council veto to kill the mission because of Guatemala's ties to Taiwan.

Under the peace agreements, the Guatemalan army is to cut its numbers and about 3,000 guerrillas from the Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG) are to go to assembly points, disarm and be integrated into civilian life.
The U.N. observers are to monitor some eight URNG camps at the assembly points, Eckhard said, as part of U.N.-brokered peace accords that ended more than three decades of warfare.
In Beijing on Tuesday, China confirmed reports that Guatemala, after a week of secret negotiations, had agreed to stop supporting moves aimed at getting Taiwan admitted to the United Nations.
"They pledged to respect the provisions of Resolution 2758 of the General Assembly and to use it as a guide to relevant actions in the United Nations," Foreign Ministry spokesman Shen Guofang said.
That 1971 resolution expelled Taipei from the world body, replacing it with Beijing as the representative of China.
"According to this resolution, Guatemala cannot support Taiwan's actions to regain entry to the United Nations," Shen told reporters.

For the past four years Guatemala has been among a number of small countries, mainly from Central America, the Caribbean and Africa, that have sought the inscription of a new General Assembly agenda item aimed at establishing a committee to consider U.N. membership for Taiwan.
But China did not insist that Guatemala break diplomatic relations with Taiwan.
Nor was there a public apology from Guatemala for inviting Taiwan's foreign minister John Chang to the December 29 peace accord signing ceremonies, as China had once wanted.
